1.x: Approximately 2 years pass between the events of Ch 1 & Ch 2. Herod the Great (73-4 BC) was the Roman-appointed king of Judea at the time of Jesus’ birth. He was appointed by the Roman Senate, with support from Mark Antony and later Augustus, the first Roman Emperor (27 BC) after defeating Mark Antony (31 BC). Herod took Jerusalem by force with Roman backing, and ruled as a client king under Rome. He was a brilliant builder and significantly expanded the Second Temple in Jerusalem, which was completed after his death (Jn 2:20). He ruled ruthlessly, murdering his own wife, several sons, and other relatives. Herod was Idumean (Edomite) on his father’s side. Edomites are Esau’s descendants (Gen 36:1). His father, Antipater, came from Idumea (Edom). His family practiced Judaism & he followed Jewish customs (at least publicly). Wise men (Greek “magoi,” plural of magos) referred to priests and experts in mysteries in Persia & Babylon (Dan 1:20; 2:2,10,27,etc), but by this time it applied to a wide range of people whose practices included astrology, dream interpretation, study of sacred writings, the pursuit of wisdom, and magic.

2.x: The wise men would likely have been familiar with OT prophecy (Num 24:17) through interaction with Jews in Babylon since the times of Daniel (Dan 5:11). Messianic Jews (Jews that accept Christ) believe that these Magi were Jewish sages, not pagan ones, as Babylon was still the place of residence for the majority of the Jewish community at the time. They also believe that the “star” was a manifestation of YHWH’s Sh’khinah (the same Divine Spirit that filled the Holy of Holies, marking the arrival of the Son of Man). The word “worship” comes from the Greek word “proskyneo”, and it can mean to make obeisance to, do reverence to, to worship, or to do homage to superiors. The wise men likely traveled with a large number of attendants and guards for the long journey, which would have taken several weeks. For example, if they had come from Babylon by the main trade route of about 800 miles (1,288km), averaging 20 miles per day, the trip would have taken about 40 days.

6.x: It cites Micah 5:2. The book of Micah was written around 740-700BC. The prophet himself is dated by Micah 1:1: “The word of the LORD that came to Micah… in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” (KJV). These kings ruled in: (1) Jothan (~750-735BC), (2) Ahaz (~735-715BC), (3) Hezekiah (~715-686BC). Micah prophesied during the rise of the Assyrian empire & the fall of the northern kingdom of Israel in 722BC. He warned about judgement on Israel (north) & Judah (south), about corruption & injustice, and about a future restoration.

7.x: “Then Herod.. privily..”: “Privily” means secretly or in private. Herod did not want his court, the Jewish populace, or the chief priests to know the details of his meeting with the Magi. Publicly, he maintained a facade of composure, but privately, he was plotting. “..what time the start appeared..”: Herod needed a precise timeline to calculate the exact age of the child. By determining when the celestial star first became visible in the East, he could estimate how long the child had been alive. This sets the groundwork for v.26, where Herod later orders the execution of all male children in Bethlehem from two years old and under, according to the time he had precise knowledge of from the Magi.

8.x: “..when ye have found him, bring me word again..”: Herod attempts to use the innocent Wise Men as unwitting intelligence informants for the Roman-backed state apparatus. “...that I may come and worship him also”: Herod masks his murderous intention behind the language of religious devotion.

9.x: Bethlehem was only 6 miles (9.7km) from Jerusalem, almost directly south. Ordinary stars or astronomical conjunctions do not move southward and pin-point a specific residence. This indicates the "star" was a unique, localized light manifestation (perhaps a manifestation of the Shekinah glory of God) guiding them directly to the specific house (v. 11) rather than just the general town of Bethlehem.

10.x: "...they rejoiced with exceeding great joy”: In the original Greek, Matthew stacks multiple words of intensity (echarēsan charan megalēn sphodra), literally translated as "they rejoiced a great joy exceedingly." The intense joy of the Magi contrasts sharply with the trouble and fear experienced by Herod and all Jerusalem (v. 3). Those who seek Christ with a sincere heart find overwhelming joy, while those who resist His kingship experience unrest.

11.x: The wise men did not arrive at the time of Jesus’ birth in a manger, but up to two years later, when Jesus was living in a house. Here Jesus is worshipped as an infant. Oneness Christians believe that the Father was dwelling in His Son from conception (Isa 9:6), literally “God with us” (Mt 1:23). However, during the early post-apostolic years, there were massive debates as to at which point the Father indwelt the Son. Some taught the Father changed modes and turned into the Son (modalism from “modes”, or also called sabellianism), others taught that the Father indwelt the Son from conception (monarchianism from monarchia=”one rule”), others taught that Jesus was “adopted” and indwelt at his baptism, others at his resurrection (dynamic monarchianism), & others began to separate God the Father from His Word, creating two distinct, divine Gods, one unbegotten, and another begotten and inferior to the Father (Justin Martyr in his “First Apology 13” & “Dialogue with Trypho 56”, ~150AC, early stages of the Trinity). Tertullian left the Roman church in ~207AC. Then in ~213AC, he wrote “Against Praxeas”, who was a Oneness preacher. In this work, Tertullian admits that Monarchians(Oneness) like Praxeas are the majority of believers at this time. This is also the first time the word “Trinity” is used to describe God. Tertullian is the father of the Trinitarian language used today, even though he is considered a heretic by modern Trinitarians. Tertullian criticizes Praxeas for his Oneness theology and for his influence on the Roman Bishop (suggesting the Roman Bishop, most likely Victor, was Oneness as well). In fact, evidence strongly suggests that Callistus I was the last Oneness Bishop in Rome in 222AC. And the very first “anti-pope” was actually Hippolytus of Rome, a Trinitarian who criticized the Roman Bishops Zephyrinus(199-217AC) and Callistus(217-222AC) (whom Catholicism falsely labels as “Popes”) for their Oneness theology in his work “Refutation Of All Heresies” (~220AC). Do not trust what Catholic or Trinitarian scholars tell you about Zephyrinus and Callistus, they’ll try to downplay their Oneness theology. But if you read for yourself, you’ll see that Hippolytus(the first anti-pope) explicitly says: “Callistus alleges that the Logos(the Word) Himself is Son, and that Himself is Father; and that though denominated by a different title, yet that in reality He is one indivisible spirit. And he maintains that the Father is not one person and the Son another, but that they are one and the same; and that all things are full of the Divine Spirit, both those above and those below. And he affirms that the Spirit, which became incarnate in the virgin, is not different from the Father, but one and the same. And he adds, that this is what has been declared by the Saviour: Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? John 14:2 For that which is seen, which is man, he considers to be the Son; whereas the Spirit, which was contained in the Son, to be the Father. For, says (Callistus), I will not profess belief in two Gods, Father and Son, but in one. For the Father, who subsisted in the Son Himself, after He had taken unto Himself our flesh, raised it to the nature of Deity, by bringing it into union with Himself, and made it one; so that Father and Son must be styled one God, and that this Person being one, cannot be two. And in this way Callistus contends that the Father suffered along with the Son; for he does not wish to assert that the Father suffered, and is one Person, being careful to avoid blasphemy against the Father. (How careful he is!) senseless and knavish fellow, who improvises blasphemies in every direction, only that he may not seem to speak in violation of the truth, and is not abashed at being at one time betrayed into the tenet of Sabellius, whereas at another into the doctrine of Theodotus” (Hippolytus, Refutation Of All Heresies, Book 9, Ch 7). The writings of Oneness teachers were destroyed, but we can still assemble the puzzle through the writings of their Trinitarian enemies attacking them. “Gold, frankincense, and myrrh”: it is assumed that there were three wise men due to the three gifts, but the actual number is unknown. Frankincense is resin used ceremonially for the only incense permitted on the altar (Ex 30:34). Myrrh is sap used in incense, perfume, and as a stimulant tonic. The gifts were likely used providentially to support the family in their flight to Egypt (Mat 2:13-15).

12.x: "Being warned of God" translates the single Greek verb chrēmatisdenthes, which specifically means to receive a divine command, oracle, or revelation. God directly communicated with these Gentile Magi through a supernatural dream. In the opening chapters of Matthew, God frequently uses dreams to guide, direct, and protect His people (e.g., Joseph in 1:20, 2:13, 2:19, 2:22). "...that they should not return to Herod”: The divine warning exposed Herod's true motives. God revealed to the Magi that the king’s professed desire to "worship" was a lie designed to locate and assassinate the child Messiah.

16.x: Bethlehem in the time of Herod was a very small village. Scholars estimate around ~300-500 people. If we take into consideration the normal birth rates in ancient times, and filter out only children of age 0-2, the likely number of infants murdered is probably around ~10 to 20 boys. Although this is not recorded by extra biblical historians, it does match Herod’s personality, who executed his own wife (Mariamne) & several of his own sons. He also ordered mass arrest before his death, so killing a small number of infants would fit his character. And since this rural event occurred at such a small village, perhaps Josephus did not find it relevant enough to record.

19.x: From the Jewish historian Josephus (in Antiquities of the Jews), we know that Herod died shortly after a lunar eclipse and before Passover. Scholars identify this eclipse as March 13, 4BC (lunar eclipse). Jesus was born before Herod died, so Jesus must have been born before 4BC. The error comes from Dionysius Exiguss (6th century, ~525AC). He created the calendar system we use today (Anno Domini, “Year of the Lord”). He tried to calculate the year Jesus was born set as 1AC. However, he miscalculated. He either misdated Herod’s date, used incomplete or inaccurate historical records, or possibly misunderstood Roman dating systems. By the time the error was discovered, the system was already widely used, it would have been too disruptive to change. But this places Jesus’ birth at around 6-4BC.

22.x: When Herod the Great died in 4BC, his kingdom was divided by the Romans among his sons: (1) Herod Archelaus was given the territories of Judea, Samaria & Idumea. This included Jerusalem & the temple. Josephus describes him as harsh, incompetent, and violent. For example, shortly after taking power, he ordered the killing of ~3,000 Jews during Passover unrest, so it makes sense that Joseph would be afraid to go there. (2) Herod Antipas ruled over Galilee & Perea. He ruled during much of Jesus’ ministry in Galilee. Executes John the Baptist and interacts with Jesus. (3) Philip the Tetrarch ruled over Iturea, Trachonitis, & Northern/eastern regions. He had a more peaceful rule. He also built Caesarea Philippi, an ancient cult center. It featured a famous grotto/cave of Pan (a fertility god, half-man half-goat), with shrines, niches carved into the cliff face for statues and idols, temples, and altars. Worship included rituals to Pan, the nymphs, Zeus, and earlier Canaanite gods like Baal. Philip, ruling a mostly non-Jewish territory, tolerated and even supported the existing pagan infrastructure as part of his loyalty to Rome. This is where Peter gives his confession of faith and is given the keys of heaven (Mt 16:13-20).

23.x: Nazareth was a relatively small village 70 miles north of Jerusalem, with a very low reputation (population estimates vary from 200 to 1,600). Luke 1:26-27 and 2:39 indicate that Joseph and Mary had earlier come from Nazareth. “He shall be called a Nazarene”: Matthew is not quoting any specific OT prophecy but is probably saying that the OT prophets foretold that the Messiah would be despised (“a reproach of men, and despised of the people” [Ps 22:6 KJV], “to Him whom man despiseth, to Him whom the nation abhorreth” [Isa 49:7 KJV]), comparable to the way in which the town of Nazareth was despised in the time of Jesus (“Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” [Jn 1:46 KJV]). Matthew may also have intended a wordplay connecting the word “Nazareth” to the OT messianic prophecy in Isa 11:1 (“And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” [Isa 11:1 KJV]) since “Nazareth” sounds similar to the word for “branch” in Hebrew (“Netser”), Matthew could be saying this “Nazarene” (Netser-ing) is the prophesied branch of Jesse.

3-5.x: The chief priests were mostly Sadducees & the scribes primarily Pharisees (sometimes referred to as “lawyers”). As experts of the Law, they knew exactly where the Messiah was to be born, but lacked the faith to accompany the wise men to the place where he was.

13-15.x: From Bethlehme to the nearest Egyptian-controlled border (near Gaza/Rafah area) it was roughly 40-65 miles. This was the minimum to escape Herod’s jurisdiction. To a more practical refuge like Pelusium (eastern Nile Delta) or further, it would be about 100-200 miles. To traditional sites like the Nile region, Cairo area, or Alexandria (where many Jews lived), it was about 250-350 miles. Average daily progress for a family with an infant, donkey, rests for water/feeding, and terrain, is likely 10-20 miles per day. They left “by night” urgently, but probably switched to daytime travel for safety afterward. This would have taken them about 3-6 days to reach the nearest Egyptian border, about 8-10 days to reach Pelusium, and 2-4 weeks or more to reach deeper sites like the Nile or Cairo. “Out of Egypt”: Matthew is citing Hosea 11:1 which speaks of God leading Israel out of Egypt. Matthew, throughout his book, portrays Jesus as the new Israel. While the old Israel failed, this Israel succeeded. Just as Moses delivered Israel from slavery under Pharaoh, so Jesus will deliver humanity from the slavery of sin.

17-18.x: Matthew cites Jeremiah 31:15. Jeremiah was a major prophet of Judah (7th-6th century BC). He lived during the fall of Jerusalem (586BC) and the Babylonian exile. He warned about judgement and also spoke of a future restoration. Rachel was the wife of Jacob (who was renamed “Israel”). The two are the parents of the 12 tribes of Israel (although Rachel only birthed Benjamin, and the youngest: Joseph, the dreamer). But as the mother of Israel, she is used symbolically as the “mother” of the nation mourning her descendants. Ramah was a town near Jerusalem in the territory of Benjamin. In Jeremiah’s time, people were taken from Ramah into Babylon. Matthew uses this prophecy to show that the grief in Bethlehem echoes the earlier sorrow of Israel’s history during the Babylonian exile.

20-21.x: Matthew’s words here constitute an almost verbatim reenactment of Ex 4:19-20 KJV: “And the LORD said unto Moses in Midian, Go, return into Egypt: for all the men are dead which sought thy life. And Moses took his wife and his sons, and set them upon an ass, and he returned to the land of Egypt” In many ways, because Christ is the sum total of the history of Israel, he relived (in his person) much of the history of Israel as the New Israel.
